where: Section 3 (smoothing), repeated in the bullet list
problem: The chapter says add-one smoothing with idf(t) = log((N + 1) ÷ (df(t) + 1)) "avoids zero or infinite values". It does not avoid zero: when a term appears in every document, df = N, so (N + 1)/(N + 1) = 1 and idf = log(1) = 0, exactly as in the unsmoothed case. Smoothing only removes the blow-up for df very small or zero (and the division-by-zero risk), not the zero weight for an everywhere-term. A student will believe the smoothing fixes something it does not.
fix: Say: smoothing keeps idf finite when df(t) is 0 or very small; it does not remove the zero weight of a term that appears in every document, since (N + 1)/(N + 1) = 1 still gives log 0. Libraries add 1 to the whole idf, idf(t) = log((N + 1) ÷ (df(t) + 1)) + 1, so even an everywhere-term keeps a small non-zero weight.

problem: The chapter lists "log scaling" (tf = 1 + log(count)) and a separate "sublinear tf" (tf = count ÷ (count + k)). In standard NLP texts and in scikit-learn's sublinear_tf option, the name "sublinear tf" means tf = 1 + log(count). Giving the same idea two names and attaching the standard name to a different formula will confuse students who check the library documentation.
fix: Call tf = 1 + log(count) the sublinear (logarithmic) tf, and describe tf = count ÷ (count + k) separately as a saturating tf with k around 1, noting it caps the count without a logarithm.
